title: ר' יהושע בן פרחיה הנשיא

paragraphs: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perachyah, the Nasi: in the Mishnah, Avot 1:6 and Chagigah 2:2 (16a). He lived in the Hasmonean period. He, Nittai of Arbel, and Mattityahu ben Yochanan received from Yose ben Yoezer and Yose ben Yochanan of Jerusalem (Avot, chapter 1), [where the checked text names only Yehoshua and Nittai as recipients,] in the year 3560, 152 years after the Temple’s construction. When Yannai, called Alexander son of Hyrcanus, killed the sages (see above, part 1, year 3670), Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perachyah fled to Alexandria in Egypt, called Amon mi-No. His student Rabbi Shimon ben Shetach asked the king to bring him back and wrote: ‘From me, Jerusalem the holy city, to you, Alexandria: my husband dwells within you, while I sit desolate.’ He said: ‘We may infer that there is peace,’ as related at the end of Sotah, 47a. [The checked passage gives the letter and its inference. It does not say that Shimon asked the king or call him Yehoshua’s pupil.] At the end of the final chapter of Menachot, 109b, end, he said: ‘At first, anyone who told me to rise to greatness, I would bind him and put him before a lion. Now, anyone who tells me to descend from it, I throw a kettle of hot water upon him.’ See Rabbi Yehoshua ben Kefusai and Rabbi Yehudah ben Tabbai, who said this. He lived a long life and came to Jerusalem 296 years after the Temple’s construction; another version has the numeral תש״ר from the creation of the world. Yeshu the Nazarene was his student. He lived in the days of Queen Helena, who lived in Hillel’s days, about seventy years before the Temple’s destruction (Shalshelet HaKabbalah 24b, end; Sefer Nitzachon, section 348). See part 1 under the years 3560, 3724, 3761, and 3671. Ibn Yachya, page 25, erred in writing that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perachyah was a student of Hillel and Shammai and the teacher of Yeshu the Nazarene. [The checked Shalshelet OCR distinguishes a later figure whom it places in the time of Hillel and Shammai’s pupils.] I have a copy of an account of an incident in Queen Helena’s days, involving a student of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perachyah. Gelilot Eretz Yisrael [גא״י; provisional expansion] writes that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Perachyah and Yitro, Moses’ father-in-law, are buried in the town of Chittin. This requires examination.
